query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled dual-scale porosity microstructure into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will improve its mechanical integrity by inhibiting crack initiation and propagation, while preserving its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: Fully dense (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric effect but suffers from poor structural integrity and tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a sacrificial phase during alloy processing that is later selectively removed to create a dual-scale (micron- and nano-scale) porous network within the alloy.
generation.conditions: Under applied-field and pressure-field operations at room temperature and under moderate mechanical loading (compressive testing typically used for caloric materials), replicating the operational conditions where both caloric response and mechanical integrity are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual porosity structure where small, uniformly distributed pores act as crack deflection sites and energy absorbers while maintaining the lattice distortions linked to the caloric response.
generation.mechanism: The introduced porosity redistributes local stresses and interrupts crack propagation pathways, thereby enhancing compressive strength. Simultaneously, the intrinsic lattice distortions that drive the caloric phase change are left intact, preserving the material’s caloric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength (potentially on the order of tens to low hundreds of MPa relative to the fully dense alloy) with the caloric response (e.g., phase transition temperature and magnitude of caloric effect) remaining essentially unchanged.
generation.baseline: The unmodified, fully dense (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which provides a large caloric response but exhibits poor mechanical integrity and is prone to cracking.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under typical applied-field and pressure conditions at near room temperature. Results may vary if operating conditions deviate significantly (e.g., at very high temperatures or extreme loading rates) which would require additional optimization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in compressive strength and any subtle impacts on the caloric effect are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy: one set produced via conventional processing (fully dense) and a second set processed with the incorporation of a sacrificial phase that is subsequently removed to create a dual-scale porosity microstructure. Subject both sets to identical compressive tests and caloric response measurements under applied magnetic and pressure fields at room temperature.
measurements: Caloric effect characterization (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change)
Microstructural analysis (pore size distribution and crack propagation imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the porous samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., at least ~30% improvement) in compressive strength relative to the dense baseline without a reduction of more than 10% in the caloric effect, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The unique properties of the porous HECs are ascribed to the high-entropy effects and dual-porosity structures. The severe lattice distortions in the HECs lead to the low intrinsic thermal conductivity by reducing phonons’ mean free path and increasing phonon scattering. Moreover, this results in high compressive strength by inhibiting the crack generations and propagations. The dual-porosity structure possesses several small pores in high-porosity ceramics. These small pores are more efficient in scattering phonon thermal conductivity and inhibiting crack propagations, which are beneficial to improving the thermal insulation and mechanical properties of the porous HECs.
